knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

```{r model-source, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
ui <- rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("HerediaOrtiz_2014_benzopyrene"))
cat("* Citation: ", ui$reference, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0102570>\n")
```

Heredia-Ortiz and colleagues built two toxicokinetic models to interpret
biomonitoring of workers exposed to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs),
using urinary 3-hydroxybenzo(a)pyrene (3-OHBaP) as the biomarker of
benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) exposure. The headline model is a whole-body physiologically
based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model (Figure 1 of the paper). Alongside it the
authors fit a deliberately simple **single-compartment toxicokinetic model**
(Figure 2), which is the model packaged here.

In the simple model, absorbed BaP enters a whole-body pool through
route-specific first-order absorption. The pool is eliminated at a single rate
`kb`, and a route-specific fraction `alpha` of that elimination appears in urine
as 3-OHBaP (the rest leaves by other routes). The authors parameterised the
inhalation and dermal routes for the occupational cohort; the published general
equations (Appendix S1, Eqs. 27-32) also carry oral and intravenous routes,
which were not fit (direct oral exposure was deemed insignificant for these
workers and intravenous dosing is not an occupational route).

The whole-body PBPK model is **not** packaged: its human organ volumes and blood
flows are taken from Brown 1997 and Davies & Morris 1993, and its structure from
the rat PBPK model of Heredia-Ortiz & Bouchard 2013 (doi:10.1007/s10928-013-9338-9),
none of which report those values within this paper. Reconstructing it would
require substituting physiological constants from outside the paper, which would
make the model unauditable (see "Assumptions and deviations").

# Occupational context

```{r population, echo = FALSE}
pop <- ui$population
tibble::tibble(
  Field = names(pop),
  Value = vapply(pop, function(x) paste(as.character(x), collapse = "; "), character(1))
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Study population, from the model's `population` metadata.")
```

The human absorption, metabolism and elimination constants were fit to the
urinary 3-OHBaP elimination time course of a single worker (worker 4 of an
artificial shooting-target factory, over the 35-45 h after onset of a weekly
exposure) and then evaluated against three further industrial cohorts (an
artificial shooting-target factory, a carbon disk-brake plant, and a silicon
production plant repairing metallurgical furnaces). Urinary 3-OHBaP was measured
in complete voids over a work week and the following days off, corrected for
creatinine. The model carries no between-worker random effects and no residual
error: the publication fits point values by a Monte-Carlo / chi-square
procedure, so the packaged model is deterministic.

# Source trace

Every `ini()` entry carries an in-file comment naming its source location; the
table below collects them for review.

```{r source-trace, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Quantity,                               ~Value,            ~Source,
  "d/dt(depot_inh), d/dt(depot_der)",      "n/a",             "Appendix S1 Eqs. 30, 28 (dA_route/dt = -ka_route*A_route + D_route)",
  "d/dt(body_inh) + d/dt(body_der)",       "n/a",             "Appendix S1 Eq. 31 (dB/dt = -kb*B + sum ka_route*A_route)",
  "d/dt(urine)",                           "n/a",             "Appendix S1 Eq. 32 (dU/dt = alpha*kb*B)",
  "ka_inh (inhalation absorption rate)",   "48.35e-3 /h",     "Results, single-compartment model",
  "ka_der (dermal absorption rate)",       "61.81e-3 /h",     "Results, single-compartment model",
  "kb (whole-body elimination rate)",      "198.26e-3 /h",    "Results, single-compartment model",
  "alpha_inh (urinary recovery, inhal.)",  "3.99e-2",         "Results, single-compartment model",
  "alpha_der (urinary recovery, dermal)",  "1.64e-2",         "Results, single-compartment model"
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Source trace for every equation and parameter in the model file.")
```

## Units and dimensional analysis

Amounts are in nmol and time in hours; the model is linear, so the absolute dose
scale is arbitrary and every output scales proportionally with the absorbed
dose. Each ODE term must have units of nmol/h.

```{r units-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Symbol,                      ~Units,  ~Note,
  "depot_inh, depot_der",       "nmol",  "absorbed BaP awaiting first-order absorption",
  "body_inh, body_der",         "nmol",  "route shares of the whole-body BaP pool (sum = Eq. 31 B)",
  "urine",                      "nmol",  "cumulative urinary 3-OHBaP",
  "ka_inh, ka_der, kb",         "1/h",   "first-order rate constants",
  "falpha_inh, falpha_der",     "-",     "unitless urinary recovery fractions",
  "ka_route * depot_route",     "nmol/h","absorption flux into the body pool",
  "kb * body_route",            "nmol/h","elimination flux from the body pool",
  "ohbap_urine_rate",           "nmol/h","urinary 3-OHBaP appearance rate (proportional to void concentration)"
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Units of every symbol in the ODE system.")
```

Checking `d/dt(body_der) = ka_der * depot_der - kb * body_der`: both terms are
(1/h)(nmol) = nmol/h, matching the state's nmol/h derivative. `d/dt(urine) =
alpha * kb * body` is (unitless)(1/h)(nmol) = nmol/h.

# Structural and mass-balance checks

Three properties follow from the equations rather than from any fitted value, so
they are exact (to solver tolerance) and catch a sign error, a dropped term or a
mis-typed constant immediately. The model carries no random effects, so every
check is deterministic.

```{r helpers}
mod <- readModelDb("HerediaOrtiz_2014_benzopyrene")

# A single absorbed bolus of `D` nmol by one route, observed on a fine grid long
# enough for the body pool to clear (body half-life ~ 3.5 h).
single_route <- function(route = c("der", "inh"), D = 1000, tmax = 600) {
  route <- match.arg(route)
  cmt <- if (route == "der") "depot_der" else "depot_inh"
  ev <- rxode2::et(amt = D, cmt = cmt, time = 0) |>
    rxode2::et(seq(0, tmax, by = 0.25))
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, returnType = "data.frame")
}

kb <- 0.19826
alpha_inh <- 0.0399
alpha_der <- 0.0164
```

```{r mass-balance}
der <- single_route("der", D = 1000)
inh <- single_route("inh", D = 1000)

# 1. Mass balance (Eq. 32 integrated): the cumulative urinary 3-OHBaP from a
#    single-route absorbed dose equals alpha_route * dose exactly, because all of
#    the absorbed dose is eventually eliminated through the body pool at rate kb.
U_der <- tail(der$urine, 1)
U_inh <- tail(inh$urine, 1)
stopifnot(
  abs(U_der - alpha_der * 1000) / (alpha_der * 1000) < 1e-6,
  abs(U_inh - alpha_inh * 1000) / (alpha_inh * 1000) < 1e-6
)

# 2. Elimination rate kb, isolated by dosing straight into the body pool so the
#    (slower) absorption step is bypassed: the pool then decays at exactly kb.
body_bolus <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod,
  rxode2::et(amt = 1000, cmt = "body_der", time = 0) |> rxode2::et(seq(0, 100, by = 0.25)),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)
late <- body_bolus[body_bolus$time %in% c(20, 40), ]
k_est <- -(log(late$body[2]) - log(late$body[1])) / (40 - 20)
stopifnot(abs(k_est - kb) < 1e-4)

# 3. The urinary-rate peak time matches the one-compartment closed form
#    log(kb/ka)/(kb - ka).
tpk_der <- der$time[which.max(der$ohbap_urine_rate)]
tpk_cf <- log(kb / 0.06181) / (kb - 0.06181)
stopifnot(abs(tpk_der - tpk_cf) < 0.5)

# 4. Flip-flop: both absorption rates (ka_der = 0.0618, ka_inh = 0.0484 /h) are
#    slower than kb (0.198 /h), so absorption is rate-limiting and the terminal
#    decay of a depot-dosed profile is governed by the smaller rate ka, not kb.
tail_der <- der[der$time %in% c(300, 350), ]
k_tail <- -(log(tail_der$body[2]) - log(tail_der$body[1])) / (350 - 300)
stopifnot(abs(k_tail - 0.06181) < 1e-4)

tibble::tibble(
  Check = c("Urinary 3-OHBaP per 1000 nmol dermal dose (nmol)",
            "Urinary 3-OHBaP per 1000 nmol inhalation dose (nmol)",
            "Elimination rate kb from a direct body dose (1/h)",
            "Dermal urinary-rate peak time (h)",
            "Terminal slope of a dermal depot dose = ka_der (1/h)"),
  Model = signif(c(U_der, U_inh, k_est, tpk_der, k_tail), 5),
  Expected = signif(c(alpha_der * 1000, alpha_inh * 1000, kb, tpk_cf, 0.06181), 5)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exact structural checks against the equations and fitted constants.")
```

Per absorbed nmol, inhalation yields about `r round(alpha_inh / alpha_der, 2)`
times more urinary 3-OHBaP than dermal exposure, the ratio of the two fitted
recovery fractions (`alpha_inh` / `alpha_der` = 0.0399 / 0.0164).

# Reproducing the workweek urinary biomarker profile

Figures 3-5 of the paper show urinary 3-OHBaP rising across a work week and
decaying over the following days off, with daily peaks and troughs driven by the
shift pattern. The shape is reproduced here by driving the model with a
realistic occupational exposure: a zero-order absorbed-dose input over each work
shift (a continuous dermal/inhalation uptake during the shift), repeated across
four workdays, followed by two days off.

```{r workweek}
# Four 8-h shifts (06:00-14:00) on days 0-3, then two days off. The absorbed
# dose per shift is an arbitrary 100 nmol delivered zero-order over 8 h (the
# model is linear, so the magnitude only scales the curve).
shift_len <- 8
dose_shift <- 100
shift_starts <- c(0, 24, 48, 72)

workweek <- function(cmt) {
  # Zero-order absorbed-dose input over each shift (amt + rate => an infusion of
  # duration amt/rate = shift_len h into the route depot), plus a fine
  # observation grid. Built as a plain event data frame.
  doses <- tibble::tibble(
    id = 1L, time = shift_starts, amt = dose_shift,
    rate = dose_shift / shift_len, evid = 1L, cmt = cmt
  )
  obs <- tibble::tibble(
    id = 1L, time = seq(0, 168, by = 0.5), amt = NA_real_,
    rate = NA_real_, evid = 0L, cmt = "urine"
  )
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, returnType = "data.frame")
}

ww_der <- workweek("depot_der")
ww_inh <- workweek("depot_inh")

ww <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(time = ww_der$time, rate = ww_der$ohbap_urine_rate, Route = "Dermal"),
  tibble::tibble(time = ww_inh$time, rate = ww_inh$ohbap_urine_rate, Route = "Inhalation")
)

ggplot(ww, aes(time, rate, colour = Route)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(shift_starts, shift_starts + shift_len),
             linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey70") +
  labs(x = "Time (h from start of work week)",
       y = "Urinary 3-OHBaP appearance rate (nmol/h)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Workweek urinary 3-OHBaP biomarker profile",
       caption = "Qualitatively reproduces the workweek shape of Figures 3-5 (Heredia-Ortiz 2014).") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r workweek-checks}
# The biomarker accumulates across the week: each workday's peak is higher than
# the previous day's, and after exposure ends it decays monotonically.
daily_peak <- function(s, day) {
  w <- s[s$time >= day * 24 & s$time < (day + 1) * 24, ]
  max(w$ohbap_urine_rate)
}
peaks_der <- vapply(0:3, function(d) daily_peak(ww_der, d), numeric(1))

# Post-exposure decay: after the last shift ends (t = 80 h) the rate falls.
post <- ww_der[ww_der$time >= 96, ]
stopifnot(
  all(diff(peaks_der) > 0),           # biomarker builds up over the work week
  all(diff(post$ohbap_urine_rate) < 1e-9)  # monotonic decline during days off
)

tibble::tibble(
  Day = paste("Workday", 1:4),
  `Peak urinary rate (dermal, nmol/h)` = signif(peaks_der, 3)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Daily peak urinary 3-OHBaP rate builds up across the work week (dermal scenario).")
```

The delayed, days-long washout after exposure ends is the model's central
qualitative result. In this lumped model the persistence is absorption-rate
limited: both fitted absorption rates are slower than the body elimination rate
`kb`, so the slowly-emptying depots sustain urinary 3-OHBaP well into the days
off work (the "flip-flop" terminal slope checked above). This is the simple
model's counterpart to the PBPK model's explanation -- slow release of retained
BaP from adipose tissue and lungs -- and it is the behaviour the authors use to
argue that complete urine voids over a full week are needed to reconstruct
exposure.

# Route comparison

Because the two routes differ both in absorption rate (`ka`) and in urinary
recovery fraction (`alpha`), the same absorbed dose produces different urinary
magnitudes and slightly different timing. This is the ambiguity the authors
highlight: urinary 3-OHBaP alone does not cleanly identify the route of entry.

```{r route-compare}
rc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(time = der$time, rate = der$ohbap_urine_rate, Route = "Dermal (alpha = 0.0164)"),
  tibble::tibble(time = inh$time, rate = inh$ohbap_urine_rate, Route = "Inhalation (alpha = 0.0399)")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(time <= 120)

ggplot(rc, aes(time, rate, colour = Route)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (h after a single absorbed dose)",
       y = "Urinary 3-OHBaP appearance rate (nmol/h)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Route comparison for an identical absorbed dose",
       caption = "Single 1000 nmol absorbed dose by each route.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Assumptions and deviations

- **Only the simple compartmental toxicokinetic model is packaged.** The paper's
  companion whole-body PBPK model (Figure 1, Appendix S1 Eqs. 1-26) inherits its
  human organ volumes and blood flows from Brown 1997 and Davies & Morris 1993
  and its structure from the rat PBPK model of Heredia-Ortiz & Bouchard 2013;
  none of those physiological values is reported in this paper. Reconstructing it
  would mean substituting physiological constants from outside the sources, which
  would make the model unauditable, so it is left for a follow-up once those
  references are obtained.
- **Inhalation and dermal routes only.** The general equations (Eqs. 27-31) also
  carry oral and intravenous absorption compartments, but the authors fit rate
  constants only for inhalation and dermal uptake (direct oral exposure was
  deemed insignificant for the workers, and intravenous dosing is not an
  occupational route). The two unfitted routes are therefore omitted rather than
  carried with invented rate constants.
- **The whole-body pool is split by route.** Eq. 31 is a single pool `B` fed by
  all routes; the paper fits a separate urinary recovery fraction `alpha` for
  each route and simulates one route at a time. To carry both fitted `alpha`
  values in a single model, the pool is split into `body_inh` and `body_der`, so
  each route's urinary contribution uses its own `alpha`. The system is linear,
  so for any single-route exposure this is identical to Eq. 31, and the sum
  `body_inh + body_der` is the paper's `B`.
- **The observable is an excretion rate.** The measured biomarker is the urinary
  3-OHBaP concentration in each void; the model exposes the urinary appearance
  rate `ohbap_urine_rate`, which is proportional to that concentration (the
  constant of proportionality is the urine production rate, which the paper does
  not model). The cumulative `urine` state gives the total excreted.
- **Dose scale is arbitrary.** The absorbed-dose inputs are in nmol but the model
  is linear; the paper notes that changing the exposure concentration or exposed
  surface only scales the simulated urinary profile without altering its shape,
  so the absolute magnitude of the dose inputs in this vignette carries no
  physiological claim.
- **Deterministic, no residual error.** The publication fits point values by a
  Monte-Carlo / chi-square procedure and reports no inter-individual or residual
  variability, so the packaged model carries no `eta` terms and no residual
  error.
- **Rate constants are kept on the linear scale.** `ka_inh`, `ka_der` and `kb`
  are fixed mechanistic rate constants reported as point values, not estimated
  population-PK parameters, so they are written on the natural (linear) scale per
  the mechanistic-parameter convention. `checkModelConventions()` emits an
  advisory suggesting a log-transformed `lka_inh` / `lka_der`; that is the
  expected false positive for a deterministic mechanistic model of this class.
```
